douglas-fir.name: Douglas Fir
douglas-fir.description: The tallest conifer in the pine family and iconic tree of the Pacific Northwest
douglas-fir.about: The Douglas Fir is the tallest tree in the Pinaceae family and one of the most iconic trees of the Pacific Northwest. Native to western North America, it's abundant throughout Woodinville and can reach heights of 200-300 feet in ideal conditions. The tree is easily recognizable by its distinctive cones with three-pronged bracts and flat, soft needles.
douglas-fir.nativeHabitat: Western North America, from British Columbia to California, sea level to 5,000 feet elevation
douglas-fir.landscapingUses: Excellent as specimen tree, windbreak, or privacy screen. Provides year-round beauty and wildlife habitat. Widely used in forestry and landscaping.
douglas-fir.leavesDescription: Flat, soft needles 1-3.5 cm long with two white stomatal bands underneath
douglas-fir.barkDescription: Thick, deeply furrowed, reddish-brown to gray-brown with resin blisters
douglas-fir.fruitDescription: Distinctive cones 5-11 cm long with three-pronged bracts extending from cone scales
douglas-fir.growingConditions: Douglas Firs thrive in the moist, temperate climate of Woodinville. They prefer well-drained soils and can tolerate both full sun and partial shade. These trees are well-adapted to the Pacific Northwest's wet winters and dry summers.
douglas-fir.locationInfo: Douglas Firs are found throughout Woodinville in both natural forested areas and residential landscapes. Look for them in local parks, along hiking trails, and in many neighborhood yards where they provide year-round beauty and privacy.
douglas-fir.wildlifeValue: These trees provide important habitat for birds, squirrels, and other wildlife. Their seeds are a food source for many animals, and their dense foliage offers excellent shelter and nesting sites. The tree supports a diverse ecosystem.

spring.title: Spring Characteristics
spring.description: In spring, Douglas Firs show new growth with bright green tips on their branches. The new needles are softer and lighter in color, creating a fresh, vibrant appearance.
characteristics: Contrast between old and new foliage

summer.title: Summer Characteristics
summer.description: Summer brings the Douglas Fir to its full glory. The needles are at their deepest green, and the tree provides excellent shade and cooling.

fall.title: Fall Characteristics
fall.description: While Douglas Firs don't change color like deciduous trees, fall brings subtle changes. The cones mature and begin to open, releasing their seeds.
characteristics: Mature cones open and release seeds
Subtle color variations in older needles

winter.title: Winter Characteristics
winter.description: Winter showcases the Douglas Fir's resilience and beauty. The tree maintains its green color against the gray winter sky, and when snow falls, it creates a stunning contrast.
characteristics: Dense foliage offers shelter from elements

photography.intro: Capturing the beauty of Douglas Firs throughout the seasons requires understanding their unique characteristics and the best times to photograph them.
tips: Golden Hour: Early morning or late afternoon light creates warm, dramatic shadows
Overcast Days: Soft, even lighting brings out the texture of bark and needles
After Rain: Water droplets on needles create beautiful macro opportunities
Winter Snow: Snow-covered branches create stunning contrast
composition: Include the distinctive bark texture in close-ups
Capture the tree's height by shooting upward
Use the tree as a backdrop for seasonal elements

bigleaf-maple.name: Bigleaf Maple
bigleaf-maple.description: The majestic broadleaf tree with the largest leaves of any maple
bigleaf-maple.about: The Bigleaf Maple is one of the most distinctive trees in the Pacific Northwest, known for its enormous leaves that can reach up to 12 inches across. This deciduous tree provides spectacular fall color and is a favorite among wildlife and photographers. It's the largest maple species in North America.
bigleaf-maple.soilPreference: Moist, well-drained soils, tolerates various conditions
bigleaf-maple.nativeHabitat: Pacific Northwest coastal and mountain forests, from sea level to 5,000 feet elevation
bigleaf-maple.landscapingUses: Excellent as specimen tree, provides shade and fall color. Great for wildlife habitat and erosion control.
bigleaf-maple.leavesDescription: Large, lobed leaves up to 12 inches across, bright green in summer, golden yellow in fall
bigleaf-maple.barkDescription: Grayish-brown, smooth when young, becoming furrowed with age
bigleaf-maple.fruitDescription: Paired winged seeds (samaras) that spin as they fall
bigleaf-maple.growingConditions: Bigleaf Maples prefer moist, well-drained soils and are commonly found in riparian areas and mixed forests. They tolerate shade well and are often found growing alongside conifers.
bigleaf-maple.locationInfo: Look for Bigleaf Maples throughout Woodinville's forested areas, particularly along streams and in mixed forests. They're common in local parks and natural areas.
bigleaf-maple.wildlifeValue: These trees provide excellent habitat for birds and small mammals. Their large leaves offer shelter, and the seeds are eaten by various wildlife species. The tree supports a diverse ecosystem.

spring.title: Spring Characteristics
spring.description: Spring brings fresh green leaves to Bigleaf Maples. The large, lobed leaves emerge bright green and create a lush canopy that provides excellent shade.

summer.title: Summer Characteristics
summer.description: Summer is when Bigleaf Maples are at their most lush. The large leaves create dense shade and the tree provides excellent cooling for the forest floor.

fall.title: Fall Characteristics
fall.description: Fall brings the Bigleaf Maple's most spectacular display. The large leaves turn brilliant golden yellow, creating stunning fall color that lights up the forest.

winter.title: Winter Characteristics
winter.description: Winter reveals the Bigleaf Maple's branching structure. The tree is bare but still provides habitat for wildlife and interesting photographic opportunities.

photography.intro: Bigleaf Maples offer excellent photographic opportunities throughout the year.
tips: Fall Color: Capture the brilliant golden leaves
Leaf Details: Focus on the large, distinctive leaves
Branching Pattern: Winter reveals interesting structure
Seasonal Changes: Document the dramatic transformations
composition: Emphasize the large leaf size in close-ups
Include the distinctive lobed leaf shape
Capture the golden fall color against green conifers
Look for interesting light patterns through the leaves

western-red-cedar.name: Western Red Cedar
western-red-cedar.description: The iconic evergreen of Pacific Northwest forests
western-red-cedar.about: Western Red Cedar is one of the most important trees in Pacific Northwest forests and is abundant throughout Woodinville. This magnificent evergreen can reach heights of 200-230 feet and is easily recognizable by its distinctive scale-like foliage and aromatic wood.
western-red-cedar.soilPreference: Moist, well-drained soils, tolerates wet conditions
western-red-cedar.nativeHabitat: Pacific Northwest forests, from sea level to 3,000 feet elevation
western-red-cedar.landscapingUses: Excellent as specimen tree, windbreak, or privacy screen. Provides year-round beauty and wildlife habitat. Widely used in forestry and landscaping.
western-red-cedar.leavesDescription: Scale-like foliage in flattened sprays, dark green above, lighter below
western-red-cedar.barkDescription: Reddish-brown, fibrous, and stringy with age
western-red-cedar.fruitDescription: Small, woody cones 8-12 mm long with 4-6 scales
western-red-cedar.growingConditions: Western Red Cedars thrive in the moist, temperate climate of Woodinville. They prefer well-drained soils and can tolerate both full sun and partial shade. These trees are well-adapted to the Pacific Northwest's wet winters and dry summers.
western-red-cedar.locationInfo: Western Red Cedars are found throughout Woodinville in both natural forested areas and residential landscapes. Look for them in local parks, along hiking trails, and in many neighborhood yards where they provide year-round beauty and privacy.
western-red-cedar.wildlifeValue: These trees provide important habitat for birds, squirrels, and other wildlife. Their dense foliage offers excellent shelter and nesting sites. The tree supports a diverse ecosystem and is particularly important for forest birds.

summer.title: Summer Characteristics
summer.description: Summer brings the Western Red Cedar to its full glory. The scale-like foliage is at its deepest green, and the tree provides excellent shade and cooling.

fall.title: Fall Characteristics
fall.description: While Western Red Cedars don't change color like deciduous trees, fall brings subtle changes. The cones mature and the tree prepares for winter.
characteristics: Mature cones open and release seeds
Subtle color variations in older foliage

winter.title: Winter Characteristics
winter.description: Winter showcases the Western Red Cedar's resilience and beauty. The tree maintains its green color against the gray winter sky, and when snow falls, it creates a stunning contrast.
characteristics: Dense foliage offers shelter from elements

pacific-madrone.name: Pacific Madrone
pacific-madrone.description: The distinctive broadleaf evergreen of Pacific Northwest
pacific-madrone.about: Pacific Madrone is a unique broadleaf evergreen tree native to the Pacific Northwest and is found throughout Woodinville. This distinctive tree can reach heights of 50-100 feet and is easily recognizable by its smooth, reddish bark that peels away in thin sheets.
pacific-madrone.growthRate: Slow to moderate, 1-2 feet per year
pacific-madrone.soilPreference: Well-drained, acidic soils, tolerates poor soils
pacific-madrone.waterNeeds: Low to moderate, drought tolerant once established
pacific-madrone.nativeHabitat: Pacific Northwest coastal areas, from sea level to 3,000 feet elevation
pacific-madrone.landscapingUses: Excellent as specimen tree, provides year-round interest. Great for wildlife habitat and erosion control.
pacific-madrone.leavesDescription: Leathery, dark green leaves 3-6 inches long, oval to elliptical
pacific-madrone.barkDescription: Smooth, reddish-brown bark that peels in thin sheets
pacific-madrone.fruitDescription: Small, round, orange-red berries 1/4 inch in diameter
pacific-madrone.growingConditions: Pacific Madrones thrive in the temperate climate of Woodinville. They prefer well-drained soils and can tolerate both full sun and partial shade. These trees are well-adapted to the Pacific Northwest's wet winters and dry summers.
pacific-madrone.locationInfo: Pacific Madrones are found throughout Woodinville in both natural forested areas and residential landscapes. Look for them in local parks, along hiking trails, and in many neighborhood yards where they provide year-round beauty and interest.
pacific-madrone.wildlifeValue: These trees provide important habitat for birds and other wildlife. Their berries are a food source for many animals, and their dense foliage offers excellent shelter and nesting sites.

summer.title: Summer Characteristics
summer.description: Summer brings the Pacific Madrone to its full glory. The leathery leaves are at their deepest green, and the tree provides excellent shade and cooling.

fall.title: Fall Characteristics
fall.description: Fall brings the Pacific Madrone's most spectacular display. The berries ripen to bright orange-red, creating a stunning contrast with the dark green leaves.

winter.title: Winter Characteristics
winter.description: Winter showcases the Pacific Madrone's unique beauty. The tree maintains its green leaves against the gray winter sky, and the smooth, reddish bark creates a striking contrast.
characteristics: Dense foliage offers shelter from elements

vine-maple.name: Vine Maple
vine-maple.description: The graceful understory maple of Pacific Northwest forests
vine-maple.about: Vine Maple is a small, graceful deciduous tree native to the Pacific Northwest and is common throughout Woodinville. This distinctive tree typically grows 15-25 feet tall and is easily recognizable by its multi-stemmed growth habit and brilliant fall colors.
vine-maple.soilPreference: Moist, well-drained soils, tolerates various conditions
vine-maple.nativeHabitat: Pacific Northwest forests, from sea level to 4,000 feet elevation
vine-maple.landscapingUses: Excellent as specimen tree, understory planting, or naturalizing. Great for wildlife habitat and erosion control.
vine-maple.leavesDescription: Round, lobed leaves 3-6 inches across, bright green in summer
vine-maple.barkDescription: Smooth, grayish-brown bark when young, becoming slightly furrowed with age
vine-maple.fruitDescription: Paired winged seeds (samaras) that spin as they fall
vine-maple.growingConditions: Vine Maples thrive in the temperate climate of Woodinville. They prefer moist, well-drained soils and can tolerate both partial shade and full sun. These trees are well-adapted to the Pacific Northwest's wet winters and dry summers.
vine-maple.locationInfo: Vine Maples are found throughout Woodinville in both natural forested areas and residential landscapes. Look for them in local parks, along hiking trails, and in many neighborhood yards where they provide year-round beauty and interest.
vine-maple.wildlifeValue: These trees provide important habitat for birds and other wildlife. Their seeds are eaten by various animals, and their dense foliage offers excellent shelter and nesting sites.

summer.title: Summer Characteristics
summer.description: Summer brings the Vine Maple to its full glory. The leaves are at their deepest green, and the tree provides excellent shade and cooling.

fall.title: Fall Characteristics
fall.description: Fall brings the Vine Maple's most spectacular display. The leaves turn brilliant shades of yellow, orange, and red, creating a stunning autumn show.
characteristics: Brilliant yellow, orange, and red leaves

winter.title: Winter Characteristics
winter.description: Winter reveals the Vine Maple's graceful branching structure. The tree is bare but still provides habitat for wildlife and interesting photographic opportunities.

red-alder.name: Red Alder
red-alder.description: The fast-growing pioneer tree of Pacific Northwest
red-alder.about: Red Alder is a fast-growing deciduous tree native to the Pacific Northwest and is common throughout Woodinville. This important pioneer species can reach heights of 50-80 feet and is easily recognizable by its smooth, grayish bark and distinctive catkins.
red-alder.soilPreference: Moist, well-drained soils, tolerates wet conditions
red-alder.nativeHabitat: Pacific Northwest forests, from sea level to 3,000 feet elevation
red-alder.landscapingUses: Excellent for reforestation, erosion control, and wildlife habitat. Great for naturalizing and riparian areas.
red-alder.leavesDescription: Oval to elliptical leaves 3-6 inches long, dark green above, lighter below
red-alder.barkDescription: Smooth, grayish-white bark with horizontal lenticels
red-alder.fruitDescription: Small, woody cones 1-2 cm long, persistent through winter
red-alder.growingConditions: Red Alders thrive in the moist, temperate climate of Woodinville. They prefer moist, well-drained soils and can tolerate both full sun and partial shade. These trees are well-adapted to the Pacific Northwest's wet winters and dry summers.
red-alder.locationInfo: Red Alders are found throughout Woodinville in both natural forested areas and residential landscapes. Look for them in local parks, along hiking trails, and in many neighborhood yards where they provide year-round beauty and interest.
red-alder.wildlifeValue: These trees provide important habitat for birds and other wildlife. Their seeds are eaten by various animals, and their dense foliage offers excellent shelter and nesting sites. They also fix nitrogen in the soil, benefiting other plants.

summer.title: Summer Characteristics
summer.description: Summer brings the Red Alder to its full glory. The leaves are at their deepest green, and the tree provides excellent shade and cooling.

fall.title: Fall Characteristics
fall.description: Fall brings subtle changes to the Red Alder. The leaves turn yellow before dropping, and the cones mature.

winter.title: Winter Characteristics
winter.description: Winter reveals the Red Alder's distinctive branching structure. The tree is bare but the persistent cones and smooth bark provide winter interest.
characteristics: Smooth bark stands out in winter
